newsitem.title: INDIA: India's rulers, Congress in talks to halt crisis.
newsitem.headline: India's rulers, Congress in talks to halt crisis.

text.p: India's ruling coalition and its Congress Party foes launched last-ditch talks on Friday to avoid fresh elections by finding a successor to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, leaders of both sides said.
They said a consensus candidate for the top job could be named by the United Front before a vote of confidence scheduled for later on Friday, or soon afterwards.
"We are expecting a change in leadership," Hannan Mollah, a deputy of the Communist Party of India-Marxist, told Reuters after Deve Gowda moved the confidence motion in the lower house.
"There is an awareness that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has to be fought together."

Bitter foes during the general election campaign last year, the 15-party United Front and Congress joined hands after the polls to put an abrupt end to the rightwing Hindu nationalist BJP's 12-day stint in power.
Congress deputies said a deal was being hammered out to replace Deve Gowda in an attempt to avoid elections, which politicians said could be held by June if the impasse continued.
"Either before the vote or after, a new leader will be chosen," said Jayanthi Natarajan, a Congress deputy. "We believe the United front has already named its candidate."
Speculation centred on G.K. Moopanar, a former Congress member who left the party last year and joined the United Front, and the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh state, Chandrababu Naidu.
Congress president Sitaram Kesri initially staked a claim to power, but later said he would settle for the replacement of Deve Gowda with a new leader.
Expectations that the centre-left coalition and Congress would be able to make amends and back a joint candidate to replace Deve Gowda pushed up share prices on Friday.
News that parliament was expected to hold a special session later in April to take up the budget also spurred a rally in stock prices, officials said. The budget was announced in February.

The speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma, held a meeting with leaders of political parties early on Friday to discuss the fate of the budget. "There was general consensus that the budget should be passed," a participant in the meeting said.

The Bombay bourse's main share index, which had fallen more than two percent in early trade on the prospect of continued political uncertainty, reversed course and was up 1.06 percent to 3,636.66 points at 0950 GMT.

Shares prices were also given a lift by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, who said he was confident the investor-friendly budget for fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) would be passed despite Deve Gowda's difficulties.

Congress sparked the political crisis on March 30 when it abruptly withdrew support for Deve Gowda, saying the prime minister had tried to sideline India's oldest party and failed to stand up to the BJP.
The 542-member lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha, was set to vote on the confidence motion at around 8 p.m. (1430 GMT).
Deve Gowda's alliance of regional, leftwing and centrist parties controls 178 votes, according to updated parliament figures. Congress has 140 votes, while the BJP and its four allies control 193.
Neither Congress nor the United Front want fresh elections, which opinion surveys have shown would boost the BJP's chances of capturing power.
